sections.content:
Now I have clean data:
- t22/t27: P (9,8) → None (death), R (9,12) → (9,10). In other words, P moved (9,8)→(9,10), then R moved (9,12)→(9,10) and killed P. Or R moved first and P moved into it. Either way, when P was at (9,10) and R was at (9,12), R moved 2 tiles left toward P.
- In all other cases, R didn't move. Including t29 (P (9,4), same row, distance 8), t25 (P (9,6), distance 6), t26 (P (9,8), distance 4).
So R's trigger: P is in the same row/column, within 2 tiles (exactly 2, since 0/1 are impossible or lethal). R moves 2 tiles toward P.
Now, the solvability problem. Under this model, let me think about whether there's a way to cross R.
Key insight to check: does R's trigger require P to be in the same row or column, or is it Chebyshev distance ≤ 2? And when P is diagonal (e.g., (11,10) relative to R (9,12)), which direction does R move?
But more importantly: is there a strategy where R moves away and P slips through?
Scenario: P at (11,10). R at (9,12).
- If R triggers on diagonal (Chebyshev distance 2): R moves toward P. Direction? If R moves left (row direction): R → (9,10). Then P (11,10) is in the same column as R (9,10), distance 2 → R moves down → (11,10) → death. If R moves down (column direction): R → (11,12). Then P (11,10) is in the same row as R (11,12), distance 2 → R moves left → (11,10) → death.
- If R doesn't trigger on diagonal: P (11,10) is safe. P moves UP → (9,10): same row, distance 2 → R moves left → (9,10) → death. P moves RIGHT → (11,12): same column, distance 2 → R moves down → (11,12) → death.
So P at (11,10) is a dead end either way.
Hmm, what about P at (11,8)? R (9,12): row difference 2, column difference 4. Chebyshev distance 4 → no trigger under any model. P (11,8) → RIGHT → (11,10) (as above, dead end). P (11,8) → UP → (9,8): same row, distance 4 → no trigger. Then P (9,8) → RIGHT → (9,10): distance 2 → R → (9,10) → death.
So all paths to the right side of R are lethal. The level is unsolvable under the "R chases within 2 tiles" model. Therefore my model must be wrong somewhere.
Reconsidering: maybe R moves 2 tiles toward P only when P moves toward R (i.e., P's move reduces the distance). Check the data:
- t22: P (9,8)→(9,10): distance 4→2, reduced. R moved. ✓
- t20: P (9,4)→(9,6): distance 8→6, reduced. R didn't move. ✗ Contradiction!
So "P moves toward R" alone isn't the trigger either. Distance threshold: R moved when distance became 2; didn't move when distance was 4, 6, 8. So trigger = distance ≤ 2 (after P's move). This is consistent with all the data.
Hmm, so under the consistent model, the level appears unsolvable... unless R's move isn't always "toward P." What if R moves 2 tiles toward P only when P is in the same row or column, and R's move is... always the same direction? No, R moved left toward P.
What if R's move is "2 tiles toward P," but if P is in the same row and within 2 tiles, R moves 2 tiles in the direction away from P?? No, R moved toward P (left, P was on the left).
What if R's trigger is "P is within 2 tiles" (Chebyshev), and R moves 2 tiles in the direction of P's row/column, but P's death at t22 was because P moved into R's path? Let me re-examine t22: P (9,8)→(9,10). R (9,12). If R moves after P: R is 2 tiles right of P → R moves left → (9,10) → P's tile → death. If R moves before P: R (9,12)→(9,10), then P (9,8)→(9,10) → death. Both are consistent.
OK, another thought: what if R's move is blocked by P? That is, R tries to move 2 tiles toward P, but if P is in the way, R stops just before P, and P dies from contact? Same result.
Let me question the assumption that P must cross (9,12). What if R can be lured into a position where it blocks itself, and P goes around via the stubs? R's possible positions: (9,12)±2 in row/column direction: (9,10), (9,14), (11,12), (7,12)=B (blocked). If R is at (9,14): the corridor is blocked at (9,14) instead. P still can't cross (9,14)... same problem, just shifted. If R is at (9,10): blocks the left side. If R is at (11,12): the row 9 corridor is open! P can cross (9,12)→(9,14)→(9,16)→UP→(7,16) goal! But R at (11,12) triggers when P is in the same column within 2 tiles: P at (9,12) (distance 2) → R moves up → (9,12) → death. P at (10,12) (distance 1): if it triggers at distance 1 → R moves up → (10,12) → death.
Hmm, so what if R's trigger distance is exactly 2 (not 1)? Then: R (11,12), P (10,12): distance 1 → no trigger. P moves UP → (9,12): distance 2 → R moves up 2 tiles → (9,12) → death. Still death.
What if R only triggers when P is in the same row (not column)? Then R (11,12), P (9,12): different rows → no trigger! P can cross! And R at (11,12) is... R only moves when P is in the same row within 2 tiles: P (11,10) or (11,14) → R moves toward P → (11,10)/(11,14). If P avoids row 11 near R, R stays at (11,12) forever!
But how does R get to (11,12) in the first place? R moves down when P is in the same column... if R only triggers on the same row, R never moves down. R starts at (9,12). Dead end.
What if R triggers on same row or column, but only moves in the row direction? Then R never leaves row 9. Dead end.
Hmm, I'm stuck on theory. Let me gather more data. The key experiment: P at (11,10) — diagonal Chebyshev distance 2 from R (9,12). Does R move? This is safe (R's 2-tile move can't reach (11,10)).
Path: P (11,4) → UP (9,4) → RIGHT (9,6) → RIGHT (9,8) → DOWN (11,8) → RIGHT (11,10). 5 moves. Check R after each move (R should stay put until the last one, if it triggers at all).
If R moves: record the direction (left → (9,10), or down → (11,12)).
If R doesn't move: next, P (11,10) → UP → (9,10): same row, distance 2 → R should move left → (9,10) → P's death. Don't do that. Instead, if R doesn't move at (11,10), try P → RIGHT → (11,12): same column, distance 2 → if R moves down → (11,12) → death. Risky, but this is the crux: does R move vertically? If R moves down onto P → death (but we learn it moves vertically). If R doesn't move → P is at (11,12), R at (9,12): then P → UP → (10,12) (R is 2 above... wait, R (9,12), P (10,12): distance 1). Hmm.
Let me run the (11,10) experiment first.
